title: Why Is a 70-Person Company a Threat to Hollywood's Big Six?
excerpt: STX is ambitious. It has pushed its way into a Hollywood where creativity thins out year by year, and it plays the challenger. Can it be the future?
body:
STX is ambitious. It has pushed its way into a Hollywood where creativity thins out year by year, and it plays the challenger. Can it be the future?

Burbank, California, is known as the "media capital of the world." Warner Bros., Disney, Universal — no more than a 20-minute drive apart, business enemies living like neighbors, deciding together which films the rest of the world will see next.

A little over a year ago, a new neighbor moved in among them: STX.

STX has the top floor of the tallest building on Hollywood Boulevard. Sometimes Adam Fogelson, chairman of the STX Motion Picture Group, points out the window toward the southwest corner and tells visitors: "Look down from here and you can see Universal Pictures."

Most of Hollywood's history is visible from that same window.

Judging by the address alone, "STX Entertainment stands out among the crowd of film studios," *Variety* wrote.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607021720421rAEJcCYV2WlK3qs.jpg-w600)

STX recently beat Fox, Universal and Lionsgate at the Cannes Film Festival, winning the overseas distribution rights to *The Irishman* for $50 million. It is Martin Scorsese's new film, bringing Robert De Niro and Al Pacino together in the kind of crime story Scorsese does best. The script is still being polished, and no next steps have been announced.

The day before that deal closed, STX had paid $9 million for the U.S. and Chinese distribution rights to *Molly's Game*, Aaron Sorkin's first film as a director.

This company, not yet two years old, has stolen the spotlight from Hollywood's veterans.

The veterans like blockbusters, IP and sequels. This young upstart prefers star-led, mid-budget films — more precisely, films costing $20 million to $80 million — films with no superheroes and none of the usual special-effects spectacle, films that honestly make a genre picture and tell a story.

Hollywood has become an arena for capital and blockbusters, and blockbusters have left some audiences out in the cold. Robert Simonds, STX's founder and CEO, says: "There's a huge white space there, and in that white space you can tell stories about people — that, to me, is what real movies are."

STX also knows how much the Chinese market matters, and when it comes to selling a film to Chinese audiences more cleverly, it is no worse at it than the veterans.

"If you want to build a film company in the U.S. that can go up against Paramount, Universal and Sony, partnering with China is essential," Simonds says. In a recent interview he said more about why China weighs on him: "China doesn't just have money. China has the future." So Hony Capital, part of Legend Holdings, became STX's third-largest shareholder. The two sides meet at least once a month to work through specific projects, possible partners and other day-to-day questions.

It was that investor who pointed STX toward its partner in China: Huayi Brothers Pictures. Last March, Huayi Brothers signed a three-year deal with STX to jointly invest in, shoot and distribute no fewer than 18 films before the end of 2017. *Dragon Shakes the World*《龙震天下》, made with Jackie Chan, is one result of the STX-Huayi partnership.

So even though the name STX is a mouthful, it now turns up in Chinese entertainment news very often.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702172043KC05ZaVcLA86NiDP.jpg-w600)

We have written about this before in our *Hollywood Report* series: [the hardest thing to shake in Hollywood is its ecosystem.](http://www.qdaily.com/articles/13905.html) Technology, capital and the market — if Hollywood is a system that runs steadily, these same three forces are what make it change.

In fact all of Hollywood is changing.

Netflix and Amazon, both out of Silicon Valley, have already mounted threatening challenges. New technology has changed how people watch: for a single-digit monthly subscription, an audience can stream a great many films whenever it likes. Netflix is the clearest case and the one that frightens Hollywood most — the sheer craft of *House of Cards* proved that a video-on-demand site can make good content.

The market has moved too. More and more Hollywood films reach Chinese audiences at the same time as American ones, and the Chinese box office alone can now sometimes rescue a picture. Capital followed: most of the blockbusters that opened in China in June had Chinese money behind them.

Of the three forces changing Hollywood, STX shows its strength in the last two.

Hollywood today has two traditions. First: if you don't build theme parks and don't sell toys, if all you sell is movies, you die. Second: if you make mid-budget films, you die too. Both appeared only a decade ago, and both now rule the place.

![Concept art for a Disney Marvel theme park](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702172043ejml4KYpIMS8rD1x.jpg-w600)

The result is that Hollywood prefers big IP. These films don't draw people with a story or with the stars in them; they pull audiences into theaters with characters and plots that viewers already know by heart from novels, comics and games. Batman fighting Superman, say, or Iron Man fighting Captain America.

Grand, overblown visual spectacle has become the foundation of the blockbuster, and a film built on that foundation does not need to be good — it only needs to support a sequel. For Hollywood, the more a film costs the better. Mid-budget films can't pull a crowd; studios allow themselves one or two a year, and the main target is a gold statuette.

Shawn Levy, who directed the *Night at the Museum* films, says: "The six studios put most of their energy into superhero movies or movies that can have sequels. For the past two years, every meeting I've gone to has not been about the film itself but about what its sequel should be." A veteran producer says: "As someone who makes films, I don't like shooting nothing but sequels and franchise pictures, but what we do has to be approved by the shareholders." Each of the six studios now has a parent company above it, and the parent company decides a film's fate.

When the blockbuster strategy works, a company earns more, which is why companies keep buying studios and studios keep buying IP. But the business is getting harder, which is why Viacom is shopping Paramount around.

Some are pessimistic enough to believe the six studios can no longer make enough good content to compete: "Within three years Paramount will be gone, Sony will disappear, Fox will buy Warner Bros., and in the end only Fox, Disney and Universal will be left."

STX counts as a rebel because it leans toward mid-size films. But don't films like that make money? Robert Simonds became one of the most profitable producers in the world on the back of *The Longest Yard* and *The Waterboy*, comedies he made with Adam Sandler. Several companies wanted him to run their film divisions. He refused: the job was too hemmed in. He wanted to run things himself.

In 2011 Simonds took his idea to Bill McGlashan, a partner at the private equity firm TPG. McGlashan agreed: "There are a billion people in China and another billion in India, and they all want to see new stories."

Simonds did his own research: over the past decade, star-led mid-budget films had a gross margin of 24%, twice the average. TPG then became STX's largest shareholder — in the name STX, S is Simonds, T is TPG, and X stands for the range of projects to come.

Mid-size films are not Hollywood's mainstream now, but that does not mean they are not its direction. The films the six studios put up for the Oscars are, in fact, positioned very close to STX's. This may well be a good path: the rush to the theaters that Oscar winners set off every year proves audiences do want these films.

And no one in Hollywood doubts Adam Fogelson's nose. As chairman of Universal Pictures he saw *Ted*, which Fox had turned down, and green-lit it on the spot; it became the hit of the year. Simonds says: "The three years Adam was in charge were the most profitable in Universal's history, and everything they built on afterward he laid down." But Comcast, Universal's parent, fired Fogelson and dropped in one of its own executives to replace this producer from a film family.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607021720441f3VFYuXdeU2jaHv.jpg-w600)

When he was eight, his father, Andrew Fogelson, head of marketing at Columbia Pictures, told him: "A film needs a clear good guy and a clear bad guy, so the audience knows who to root for." That was the wisdom of Hollywood in that era: put the story at the center and make genre films that draw people in.

Twenty years ago films were still creating rich and varied stories. Now the human stories Hollywood tells can only be found on the Oscar list each year.

That does not mean there is no market for them. Fogelson made *Ted* a hit, and the first film he oversaw after joining STX, *The Gift*, came out last year: made for $5 million, it took nearly $60 million worldwide.

STX can spot a film's selling point while the project is still in development, and it controls budgets and schedules tightly. It also has one very simple, direct weapon: stars.

STX always tries to work with stars, so that its films stand out among others of the same kind. This year's big release, *Free State of Jones*, stars Matthew McConaughey. *The Irishman*, the deal it closed at Cannes, is more star-studded still. Its first co-production in China was made with Jackie Chan, and it paid $2 million to bring in Martin Campbell as director, because it wanted the film to be better.

Jackie Chan has also become STX's key to the Chinese door. Chinese audiences like special effects and big set pieces, but they also like a simple story and they like stars — and Jackie Chan is popular in both China and the U.S.

STX's "better," of course, means "better to watch" and "better to sell." Fogelson admits he has no wish to lose money making a *Fight Club* or a *Shawshank Redemption*: fine films, hard to sell.

As Simonds sees it, superhero blockbusters cost so much that they have cut the total number of films made, leaving a great deal of star talent and theater capacity idle. STX means to put that idle capacity to work.

Blockbusters earn theater chains a bigger box office, but as the president of AMC Theatres put it: "A studio only has to worry about the 16 weekends a year when its own films open. I have to worry about the schedule for all 52 weekends of the year.

"The films STX puts out — the ones that make you think, the more complicated ones — will also bring a broader, wider audience into theaters, not just 21-year-olds who came to see things blow up." Because theater chains need films of different kinds, STX has made sure its own films open on at least 3,000 screens, as the six studios do, and on the same revenue split.

STX has grown fast, and the mainstream studios can no longer ignore it. At this year's CinemaCon it appeared for the first time and again became the center of attention, announcing 10 films for 2016 and 12 for 2017 — numbers that are catching up with the six.

"All six studios hate us," Fogelson says, "because they have to explain to their bosses in New York why we can make 15 films with only seventy people."

High blockbuster costs and long production cycles have cut total output, but STX is also more nimble because it has no bosses in New York to report to. At other studios a committee debates whether to make a film, taking in the views of marketing and distribution and weighing whether the toys will sell; all of it lands on a single spreadsheet, and the studio president uses that spreadsheet to judge whether the film will earn the parent company enough.

Fogelson does some financial analysis too, of course, but he usually reaches a first decision quickly. He judges whether the film stands out within its genre; he thinks about whether he knows how to sell it; and finally he judges whether its chance of success is greater than its risk of failure.

With money secured and with the experience and the channels to produce and distribute, STX looks set to start a reformation in Hollywood.

But STX is not an outsider. Its team is "as good as a mainstream studio's": this is a new company built by people who came out of Hollywood. Besides Fogelson and Simonds, Kevin Grayson, a senior vice president of distribution at Universal, runs STX's domestic distribution; Oren Aviv, former president of marketing at Fox, joined as chief content officer; and Rich Sullivan, DreamWorks's chief financial officer, is the company's CFO. That is the key to understanding Hollywood better than Hollywood does.

![From left: Kevin Grayson, general manager of domestic distribution; Fogelson, president of the film division; Sophie Watts, general manager of the film division; and Oren Aviv, chief content officer.](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607021720461A6lBgcmYH80Wdz4.jpg-w600)

Can STX change Hollywood? No one knows yet. It is not the first rebel. In 2004 Relativity Media moved into film financing and grew step by step into a mid-size producer and distributor, doing well in Hollywood — but last year Relativity went bankrupt and restructured, and it is only now crawling out of the mud and limping forward. There were many reasons for its collapse. One was that it concentrated only on films that looked profitable, and most of them were bad films.

STX means to keep making good stories, and to sell those stories well. That is the future it has chosen.
